entry:
Carnivoran mammal of the family Ursidae.

Only eight species are extant, and they are widespread across most of the Northern Hemisphere and partially in the Southern Hemisphere, on the continents of North America, South America and Eurasia. Common characteristics include large bodies, stocky legs, long snouts, shaggy hair, plantigrade paws with five nonretractable claws and short tails.

The [[Polar bear|polar bear]] is mostly carnivorous and the [[Giant panda|giant panda]] mostly herbivorous; the other six species are omnivorous. Bears are typically solitary apart from courting individuals and mothers with their young. Most species occupy dens during winter for [[Hibernation|hibernation]] of up to 100 days, and they have an excellent [[Sense of smell|sense of smell]].

Bears have been hunted for meat and fur since prehistoric times and play a prominent role in the arts and mythology of many human societies. The IUCN lists six species as vulnerable or endangered, and poaching and trade in the most threatened populations are prohibited but continue.

British adventurer and television presenter.

A former trooper in the Special Air Service, he holds several world records in hostile environments. His wilderness survival series include *Man vs. Wild* (2006–2011) and *The Island with Bear Grylls* (2014–2019). In July 2009 he was appointed the youngest-ever Chief Scout of the United Kingdom and Overseas Territories, at age 35, and held the post until September 2024.

[[Hair]] on the jaw, chin, lips, cheeks and neck.

In humans, beards are most common among pubescent and adult males, though some women develop them in a condition called hirsutism. Beard growth is linked to dihydrotestosterone, which stimulates hair follicles in the area during [[Puberty|puberty]] and afterward; the same hormone promotes balding. Biologists classify beards as a secondary sexual characteristic that plays no direct role in reproduction. [[Charles Darwin]] first suggested in *The Descent of Man* that sexual selection might explain them, and modern biologists have reaffirmed that role.

Attitudes toward beards have varied across history. In Phoenicia, beards were arranged in tight curls, and Israelite society placed special importance on them. The Hittites and Elamites were clean-shaven, and the Sumerians often were. Several religions require or encourage beards, and some societies have associated them with masculinity, virility, wisdom and high social status. In cultures where beards are uncommon, they may be linked with poor hygiene or eccentricity.

Very large [[Bird of prey|bird of prey]] in the monotypic genus *Gypaetus*. Also called the lammergeier and ossifrage, it is the only known vertebrate whose diet consists of 70–90% bone.

Traditionally considered an [[Old World vulture]], it forms a separate minor lineage of Accipitridae with the Egyptian vulture, its closest living relative, and differs from Old World vultures by its feathered neck. It breeds on crags in high mountains from southern Europe to East Africa, the [[Indian subcontinent]], [[Tibet]] and the [[Caucasus]]. The population is declining; it has been listed as near threatened since 2014.

Machine element that constrains relative motion to the desired motion and reduces [[Friction|friction]] between moving parts.

A bearing may allow free linear movement or free rotation around a fixed axis, or it may prevent motion by controlling the normal forces on moving parts. The simplest bearing is a plain bearing, a shaft rotating in a hole with lubrication to reduce friction. In ball and roller bearings, rolling elements between races reduce sliding friction, and enclosing each element in a cage keeps the elements from rubbing against each other.

A wooden ball bearing supporting a rotating table was recovered from the Roman Nemi ships in Lake Nemi, [[Italy]], which were dated to 40 BC. [[Leonardo da Vinci]] incorporated drawings of ball bearings in a helicopter design around 1500, the first recorded use of bearings in aerospace design. The first practical caged-roller bearing was invented in the mid-1740s by horologist John Harrison for his H3 marine timekeeper.

American [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] group.

Formed in New York City in 1981, the group first played hardcore punk before making a full transition to hip-hop after the 1983 single "Cooky Puss". Their debut album, *Licensed to Ill* (1986), was the first rap album to top the *Billboard* 200 chart. They toured with [[Madonna]] in 1985. The group was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2012, the year Adam Yauch died and the group disbanded.

Marginal sea of the [[Arctic Ocean]] north of Alaska, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. Named after Sir Francis Beaufort, a hydrographer, it covers approximately 476,000 sq km, mostly over a shallow continental shelf. The [[Mackenzie River]], the longest river in [[Canada]], empties into its Canadian part.

The sea is frozen for most of the year, though climate change has greatly enlarged its ice-free area in late summer. It hosts one of the largest colonies of [[Beluga whale|beluga whales]] and is a habitat for [[Polar bear|polar bears]]. Petroleum and natural gas reserves under the shelf were discovered between the 1950s and 1980s, and exploration has since become the major human activity in the area.

Canada and the United States dispute a wedge-shaped slice of maritime boundary between Yukon and Alaska. Canada claims the boundary runs along the 141st meridian west, while the United States favors a boundary perpendicular to the coast, following a line of equidistance.

Empirical measure relating wind speed to observed conditions at sea or on land.

Francis Beaufort, a hydrographer and [[Royal Navy]] officer, devised it in 1805 while serving on *HMS Woolwich*. It was officially adopted when he became Hydrographer of the Navy in the 1830s. In 1916 its descriptions were changed from the behavior of sails to the behavior of the sea, and they were extended to land observations. Meteorologists now usually express wind speed in [[Knot (unit)|knots]] or other units, but Beaufort terminology is still sometimes used in shipping and severe weather warnings.

American animated musical film produced by Walt Disney Feature Animation (1991).

It was the first animated film to win the Golden Globe Award for Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy and the first to be nominated for the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Picture. It won Oscars for Best Original Score and Best Original Song. In 1994 it became the first Disney film adapted into a Broadway musical, and in 2002 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the United States National Film Registry.

[[Competition]] in which contestants are judged and ranked on physical and mental attributes.

Traditionally focused on physical attractiveness, most modern pageants also judge "inner beauty", including personality, intelligence, moral character and charity. Winners are generally called beauty queens, or beauty kings in male pageants. The term originally referred to the Big Four: [[Miss Universe]], Miss World, Miss International and Miss Earth, which are the most prestigious and widely broadcast.

Ancient Greek contests included the Callisteia, and one notable example on [[Lesbos]] awarded a prize to the fairest woman in the sanctuary of [[Hera]]. Modern pageants were first established in the early 20th century. Rules may set age ranges and require contestants to be unmarried. Critics argue that pageants reinforce narrow ideals of female attractiveness, while supporters credit them with contestants' confidence and economic opportunities.

Large semiaquatic [[Rodent|rodent]] of the [[Northern Hemisphere]].

Two species survive: the North American beaver (*Castor canadensis*) and the Eurasian beaver (*C. fiber*). Weighing up to 50 kg (110 lb), beavers are the second-largest living rodents after capybaras. They are herbivores that eat tree bark, aquatic plants, grasses and sedges.

Beavers build dams and lodges from branches, vegetation, rocks and mud. Their dams create ponds and [[Wetland|wetlands]] used by many other species, making beavers a keystone species.

The Eurasian species has 48 chromosomes and the North American species 40, which prevents them from interbreeding. Historically, beavers were hunted for fur, meat and castoreum, and beaver pelts were a major driver of the [[Fur trade|fur trade]]. Overhunting nearly exterminated both species before protections in the 19th and early 20th centuries. They are now listed as least concern by the IUCN.

Unit of radioactivity in the [[International System of Units]] (SI), symbol Bq.

One becquerel is defined as one event per second, on average, for aperiodic decays of a radionuclide. It is named after [[Henri Becquerel]], who shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre and Marie Curie for discovering radioactivity. It succeeded the curie, an older unit based on the activity of 1 gram of radium-226; 1 Ci = 3.7×10¹⁰ Bq. Because the becquerel is small, SI multiples such as kBq and MBq are common. A typical human body, containing roughly 0.017 g of potassium-40, produces about 4,400 decays per second.

[[Insect]] of the family Cimicidae that feeds on blood, usually at night.

Bed bugs are primarily of the genus *Cimex*, chiefly *C. lectularius* (the common bed bug) and *C. hemipterus*, which is found mainly in the [[Tropics|tropics]]. They are 1–7 mm long and hide in mattress seams and wall cracks during the day. Their bites cause itching, often as flat, reddish lesions or blisters, though systemic effects are rare. There is no evidence that they transmit infectious disease, although they may carry pathogens.

Eliminating an infestation is often difficult, because bed bugs can survive up to approximately 300 days without feeding. Treatments include heating a room to 50 °C (122 °F) for more than 90 minutes, frequent vacuuming and washing clothing at high temperatures. Infestation is rarely due to a lack of [[Hygiene|hygiene]] but is more common in high-density areas.

Fossils from Egypt show bed bugs have been human parasites for at least 3,500 years. They were nearly eradicated in developed countries after [[World War II]], but infestations have increased since the 1990s.

[[Furniture|Piece of furniture]] used for sleeping, resting and relaxing.

Most modern beds consist of a cushioned mattress on a frame, resting on a solid base such as wood slats or a sprung base. Sizes range from [[Infant|infant]]-sized cribs to king-size beds for two. Other types include the murphy bed, which folds into a wall, and the bunk bed, which provides two tiers. Bedding, including sheets, blankets and quilts, is the removable part that can be washed.

Early beds were piles of straw or other natural materials. Raising them off the ground helped avoid drafts, dirt and pests. Bedding dated to around 3600 BC was found in Sibudu Cave, South Africa. Wooden bed frames with headrests were used in [[Ancient Egypt]], and three ritual beds were found in the tombs of [[Tutankhamun]]. In the *Odyssey*, [[Homer]] describes the bed that [[Odysseus]] built from an olive tree trunk.

English Benedictine monk, author and scholar.

Known as the Venerable Bede, he spent most of his life at the twin [[Monastery|monastery]] of Monkwearmouth–Jarrow in the Kingdom of Northumbria. His most famous work, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, was completed about 731 and gained him the title "The Father of English History". His writings included biblical commentaries and work on computus, the science of calculating calendar dates, including the date of [[Easter]]. He helped popularize dating years from the birth of Christ, [[Anno Domini]]. Many historians consider him the most important scholar of antiquity between the death of [[Pope Gregory I]] in 604 and the coronation of [[Charlemagne]] in 800. Pope Leo XIII canonized him in 1899 and named him a Doctor of the Church, the first native of [[Great Britain]] to receive that designation.

Pastorally semi-nomadic [[Tribe|Arab tribes]] of the deserts of the [[Arabian Peninsula]], North Africa, the [[Levant]] and [[Mesopotamia]] ([[Iraq]]). The name comes from the Arabic *badawī*, meaning "desert-dweller". Traditionally they herd camels, sheep and goats, and most adhere to [[Islam]]. Many have adopted urban lifestyles, while others retain clan structures, poetry and music.

Solid rock that lies beneath weathered rock and loose surface deposits in the [[Earth's crust]].

The loose material above it, called regolith, includes soil. The surface where bedrock and regolith meet is known as rockhead, and exposed bedrock is an outcrop. Exposed bedrock undergoes [[Weathering|weathering]], physical or chemical, which leaves it susceptible to [[Erosion|erosion]]. Where superficial deposits are thick, bedrock can lie hundreds of meters below the surface, and identifying it is an important task in most [[Civil engineering|civil engineering]] projects.

Room in a residential or accommodation unit used primarily for [[Sleep|sleeping]].

A typical Western bedroom contains one or two [[Bed|beds]], a clothes closet, and a bedside table and dressing table, both usually with drawers. Beds and bedrooms are often designed to create barriers to [[Mosquito|mosquitoes]] and other insects, and to dampen or contain light and noise.

In the 14th century, the lower class in Europe slept on mattresses stuffed with hay. Feather-stuffed mattresses became popular in the 16th century among those who could afford them, and the first coil spring mattress was not invented until 1871. Built-in closets are less common in Europe than in North America, so freestanding wardrobes or armoires are used more there. Bedding in [[Scandinavia]] differs from that in North America, and futons are common in Japan.

British-Australian musical group (1958–2012).

Formed by brothers Barry, Robin and Maurice Gibb, the group wrote its own original material and was especially successful in the late 1960s and 1970s. Its soundtrack for *Saturday Night Fever* (1977) helped define the [[Disco|disco]] era and won five Grammy Awards, including Album of the Year. The Bee Gees have sold an estimated 120 million to 250 million records and were inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1997. Barry Gibb, Vince Melouney and Geoff Bridgford are the surviving members.

Winged insect of the [[Clade|clade]] Anthophila in the order Hymenoptera.

More than 20,000 species are known, in seven families. Over 90% of species are solitary, while honey bees, bumblebees and stingless bees are social. Unlike the closely related [[Wasp|wasps]] and ants, bees are herbivores that feed on nectar as a carbohydrate source and on [[Pollen|pollen]] for protein for their larvae. They live on every continent except [[Antarctica]], wherever insect-pollinated flowering plants grow.

Bees are best known as [[Pollination|pollinators]] and, in the case of the western honey bee, for producing [[Honey|honey]]. Humans have practiced [[Beekeeping|beekeeping]] since at least the times of ancient Egypt and [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]].

[[Genus]] of deciduous trees in the family Fagaceae.

Beeches are native to subtropical and temperate Eurasia and North America, with 14 accepted species in two subgenera. The European beech (*Fagus sylvatica*) is the most commonly cultivated species. Its timber is used for [[Furniture|furniture]], flooring, construction and plywood, and beechwood makes excellent firewood. Beech is also used to smoke Westphalian ham, andouille sausage and some cheeses.

Beeches are monoecious, with wind-pollinated catkins, and their three-angled nuts sit in spiny cupules. *Fagus* is the first diverging lineage in the evolution of Fagaceae, which includes [[Oak|oaks]] and [[Chestnut|chestnuts]]. The oldest fossils assignable to the beech lineage are 81–82 million years old pollen from the [[Cretaceous|Late Cretaceous]] of [[Wyoming]], U.S.

Meat from cattle (*Bos taurus*).

Cuts are often used for steak, while trimmings are ground for [[Hamburger|hamburgers]]. Beef contains protein, iron and vitamin B12. High consumption of red meat, especially processed, is associated with an increased risk of [[Colorectal cancer|colorectal cancer]] and [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular disease]]. Beef is a primary driver of [[Deforestation|deforestation]] and has the highest [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gas]] emissions of any agricultural product.

Humans hunted [[Aurochs|aurochs]] in prehistoric times and later domesticated them. As of 2018, the United States, Brazil and China were the largest producers. Beef is the third most widely consumed meat in the world, after pork and poultry. Some religions and cultures prohibit beef, especially Indian religions such as [[Hinduism]].

Maintenance of [[Bee|bee]] colonies, commonly in artificial hives; also called apiculture.

[[Honey bee|Honey bees]] (genus *Apis*) are the most commonly kept, though stingless *Melipona* bees are also kept. Beekeepers collect [[Honey|honey]], beeswax, propolis, bee pollen and royal jelly, and earn income from [[Pollination|crop pollination]], raising queens and selling package bees. Many operations are hobbies, while the largest are agricultural businesses. Some studies have found city-kept bees healthier than rural ones because of fewer pesticides and greater biodiversity in cities.

Spanish cave paintings dated 6,000 BCE show the earliest evidence of humans collecting honey. Evidence of beekeeping in [[Egypt]] dates from 3,100 BCE, and at least 10,000 years ago people kept wild colonies in hollow logs and woven straw baskets. In the 18th century, a movable comb hive was developed that allowed honey to be harvested without destroying the colony.

Failed 1923 [[Nazi Party|Nazi]] coup attempt in [[Munich]], Germany.

Led by [[Adolf Hitler]] and General [[Erich Ludendorff]] on November 8–9, 1923, during the [[Weimar Republic]], the putsch aimed to use Munich as a base for a march on [[Berlin]], modeled on [[Benito Mussolini]]'s March on Rome. Police halted the march on the second day. Hitler was tried for treason and sentenced to five years in Landsberg Prison, where he dictated *Mein Kampf*; he was released after nine months. The widely publicized trial gave him a national platform.

Scientific law describing the absorption of [[Light|light]] by a solution.

It is used to determine the concentration of substances in solution, stating that the amount of light a solution absorbs is directly proportional to the solution's concentration. It is expressed as A = εcl, where A is absorbance, ε the absorption coefficient, c the concentration of the absorbing substance and l the path length. The law is named after August Beer and Johann Heinrich Lambert. Forms of it date to the mid-18th century, but it took its modern form in the early 20th century.
